title: Operators
summary: Combine **values** with arithmetic, comparison, and logic.
refresher: Arithmetic **operators** calculate values, comparisons produce **booleans**, and logical operators join **conditions**. Prefer `===` so type and value must match.

operators-lesson-check-1.title: Trace arithmetic one line at a time
operators-lesson-check-1.body: This question is about following each **operator** in order. Work out one printed line, write that result down, then move to the next line.
operators-lesson-check-1.notice: `//` keeps the whole-number part, `%` keeps the remainder, and `/` keeps the decimal result.
operators-lesson-check-1.mistake: Do not round floor division. It drops the leftover part instead of rounding up.

operators-lesson-check-2.title: Between means both boundaries count
operators-lesson-check-2.body: A between check asks two questions: high enough and low enough. If both ends count, the comparison needs inclusive operators.
operators-lesson-check-2.notice: `and` means both comparisons must be true at the same time.
operators-lesson-check-2.mistake: `or` is usually too loose for a between rule because one true side is enough to enter.

operators-summary-01.title: Operators do different jobs
operators-summary-01.body: **Operators** calculate values, compare values, assign values, and combine true-or-false conditions. First decide which job the line is doing.
operators-summary-01.notice: Arithmetic makes a value. Comparison makes true or false. Assignment stores a value.
operators-summary-01.mistake: Do not treat every symbol as math. Some operators ask questions or store values.

operators-supplement-01.title: Assignment is not comparison
operators-supplement-01.body: A condition should ask whether something is true. Assignment changes a value; comparison asks whether two values match.
operators-supplement-01.notice: Use the comparison operator when an if statement is asking a yes/no question.
operators-supplement-01.mistake: A single equals sign is a common typo when the code meant to compare.

operators-authored-01.title: Zero cannot be the divisor
operators-authored-01.body: Division, floor division, and remainder all need a nonzero divisor. If the divisor can come from input or another calculation, check it before dividing.
operators-authored-01.notice: The dangerous value is the number after the division or remainder operator.
operators-authored-01.mistake: Do not assume a calculated count is safe just because the formula looks reasonable.

operators-authored-02.title: Choose storing or comparing
operators-authored-02.body: Before reading a conditional expression, ask whether the code is storing a new value or comparing existing values.
operators-authored-02.notice: Assignment changes state. Comparison produces a true-or-false answer.
operators-authored-02.mistake: Mixing these up can either stop the program or quietly send it down the wrong branch.

operators-authored-03.title: Pick the division that matches the problem
operators-authored-03.body: Division operators answer different questions. Use decimal division for averages, whole-number division for complete groups, and remainder for what is left.
operators-authored-03.example:
groups = students // seats
left = students % seats
operators-authored-03.notice: The same two numbers can produce different useful answers depending on the operator.
operators-authored-03.mistake: Do not use whole-number division when the assignment expects a decimal average.

operators-authored-04.title: Floor division drops the leftover
operators-authored-04.body: Whole-number division keeps the number of complete groups and ignores the leftover part.
operators-authored-04.notice: The leftover is not lost forever if the code also asks for the remainder.
operators-authored-04.mistake: Do not round up. Complete groups only count when they are fully filled.

operators-authored-05.title: Remainder checks divisibility
operators-authored-05.body: The remainder operator is useful when a rule depends on whether something divides evenly.
operators-authored-05.notice: Even numbers leave remainder 0 when divided by 2.
operators-authored-05.mistake: Do not compare the original number to 0 when the question is about the leftover.

operators-authored-06.title: Power has its own operator
operators-authored-06.body: When a question asks about raising a number to a power, look for the language's exponent operator or function, not a symbol that only looks mathematical.
operators-authored-06.notice: A familiar-looking symbol can mean something different in code.
operators-authored-06.mistake: Do not assume `^` means exponent just because it is used that way in some calculators or notes.

sections.title: Mathematical operators
sections.summary: Calculate values and watch how JavaScript treats numbers and strings.

blocks.body: Arithmetic **operators** calculate values, comparisons produce **booleans**, and logical operators join **conditions**. Prefer `===` so type and value must match. Combine values with arithmetic, comparison, and logic.

**Operators** work in a particular order. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, then comparisons produce **booleans** (the values `true` and `false`) that logical operators can combine. JavaScript also chooses behavior from operand types, so plus adds two numbers but joins text when either side is a **string**.

blocks.caption: Multiplication runs before addition, then strict equality tests the completed result.
Explicit conversion makes the intended operation visible.

blocks.body: Trace an expression in small pieces. For `2 + 4 * 3 === 14`, calculate `4 * 3`, add two, and compare fourteen with fourteen. Each intermediate result has both a **value** and a type.

blocks.why: Multiplication produces six before that **value** is subtracted from ten.

sections.title: Bitwise operators
sections.summary: Recognize the special operators that work on 32-bit integer patterns.

blocks.body: JavaScript has **bitwise operators**, but they are a special tool. They convert numbers to 32-bit integer patterns first, then work on the **bits**. That is useful for masks and flags, but it is not how most beginner arithmetic or conditions are written.

blocks.caption: The symbols look short, but they are not the same as logical conditions. `&`, `|`, and `^` compare bit positions. `<<` shifts bits to the left.

blocks.title: Logical operators have doubled symbols
blocks.body: Use `&&`, `||`, and `!` for **conditions**. Use bitwise operators only when the problem says bits, masks, flags, or binary representation. A single `&` where you meant `&&` is a tiny typo with a very different meaning.

sections.title: Comparison operators
sections.summary: Use strict comparisons so both type and value have to match.

blocks.title: Watch this detail
blocks.body: Loose equality may convert an operand first, so `5 == "5"` is true while `5 === "5"` is false.

blocks.why: The **variable** holds a **string**, so it is strictly unequal to the number seven.

sections.title: Conditional logic operators
sections.summary: Join conditions and keep a short checklist for dense expressions.
